properties.title: AIO Fact Check
properties.content: Question: how to check for testicular cancer Answer: To check for testicular cancer, perform a monthly self-exam, ideally in a warm shower to relax the scrotum. Feel for any lumps, bumps, or changes in size or firmness of the testicles. Also, be aware of any pain or discomfort. If you find anything unusual, see a doctor promptly. Steps for a Testicular Self-Exam:: - Warmth: Find a warm, comfortable place like a shower or bath where the scrotum is relaxed. - One testicle at a time: Hold each testicle gently between your thumb and fingers. - Feel for changes: Roll the testicle gently, feeling for any lumps, bumps, or changes in size or firmness. It's normal to have some slight asymmetry. - Repeat: Do the same for the other testicle. Important Considerations:: - Frequency: A monthly self-exam is recommended, especially for men between 15 and 35, the age range when testicular cancer is most common according to Yale Medicine. - Normal Variation: It's normal for testicles to be slightly different in size or shape. Don't panic if you notice a difference, but be aware of any new changes or lumps. - When to see a doctor: If you find any lump, swelling, or pain that is not normal for you, see a doctor immediately. Other Diagnostic Tests:: If a self-exam raises concerns, a doctor may use additional tests, including:: - Ultrasound: Uses sound waves to create images of the testicles, helping to differentiate between solid tumors and fluid-filled cysts. - Blood tests: Can detect tumor markers (chemicals released by some testicular cancers) according to Macmillan Cancer Support. - Biopsy: A surgical procedure to remove a sample of tissue for examination under a microscope to confirm the presence of cancer according to Penn Medicine. - CT scans: Can help determine if cancer has spread to other parts of the body according to the Canadian Cancer Society.

Question: how to check for testicular cancer

Answer: To check for testicular cancer, perform a monthly self-exam, ideally in a warm shower to relax the scrotum. Feel for any lumps, bumps, or changes in size or firmness of the testicles. Also, be aware of any pain or discomfort. If you find anything unusual, see a doctor promptly.
Steps for a Testicular Self-Exam::
- Warmth: Find a warm, comfortable place like a shower or bath where the scrotum is relaxed.
- One testicle at a time: Hold each testicle gently between your thumb and fingers.
- Feel for changes: Roll the testicle gently, feeling for any lumps, bumps, or changes in size or firmness. It's normal to have some slight asymmetry.
- Repeat: Do the same for the other testicle.
Important Considerations::
- Frequency: A monthly self-exam is recommended, especially for men between 15 and 35, the age range when testicular cancer is most common according to Yale Medicine.
- Normal Variation: It's normal for testicles to be slightly different in size or shape. Don't panic if you notice a difference, but be aware of any new changes or lumps.
- When to see a doctor: If you find any lump, swelling, or pain that is not normal for you, see a doctor immediately.
Other Diagnostic Tests::
If a self-exam raises concerns, a doctor may use additional tests, including::
- Ultrasound: Uses sound waves to create images of the testicles, helping to differentiate between solid tumors and fluid-filled cysts.
- Blood tests: Can detect tumor markers (chemicals released by some testicular cancers) according to Macmillan Cancer Support.
- Biopsy: A surgical procedure to remove a sample of tissue for examination under a microscope to confirm the presence of cancer according to Penn Medicine.
- CT scans: Can help determine if cancer has spread to other parts of the body according to the Canadian Cancer Society.
